title: Signal and Vector
premise: August Sandoval, a clone who inherited both the original's identity and his unsolved murder case, keeps a lonely beacon station that no one in the fleet will admit to commissioning. When the ship Halcyon returns from deep space with its crew aged backward into children, August discovers the beacon is a memory anchor — proof of the Meridian Station massacre that the ruling Concordat has erased from every record. As the fleet's fragile truce expires, August and the regressed crew must reconstruct the massacre from fragments, risking everything to prove it happened before the last witness's mind finishes unmaking itself. In the end, August broadcasts the truth at the cost of the beacon, chooses loyalty to the living over fidelity to the dead original, and finds belonging not in inherited identity but in chosen family.
about_author: Hazel Ravensworth is a former radio astronomer turned novelist who writes science fiction about people haunted by institutional silence. She lives near a decommissioned listening post and insists her best ideas arrive on frequencies no one else bothers to monitor.

chapters.title: The Beacon Nobody Ordered
chapters.summary: POV: August Sandoval. August maintains the beacon station alone, logging its transmissions to an origin he cannot trace. A supply run reveals his predecessor — the original August — died here under suspicious circumstances, a case officially closed without investigation. The emotional beat is quiet isolation sharpening into unease as August realizes even he may be part of someone's cover-up.

chapters.title: Children at the Airlock
chapters.summary: POV: August. The ship Halcyon docks unannounced; its entire crew has aged backward into children who speak in fragments of adult memories. Among them is a girl who calls August by name and by rank he never held. The beat is dread mixed with tenderness as August realizes the beacon's signal may have done this — or saved them from something worse.

chapters.title: Meridian
chapters.summary: POV: Ilsa Vey, Halcyon's navigator trapped in her eight-year-old body. Ilsa remembers a station called Meridian and eleven thousand people, but every database aboard confirms Meridian never existed. Her frustration at being disbelieved because of her size drives the chapter, ending when she finds the word MERIDIAN scratched inside August's predecessor's desk.

chapters.title: Inherited Suspects
chapters.summary: POV: August. Digging into the original's murder file, August finds three names flagged before the case was closed: a Concordat auditor, a beacon engineer, and the original himself. He interviews the engineer via long-delay comm and hears fear disguised as senility. The beat is the detective's cold thrill curdling as he understands the murder and the erased massacre are one case.

chapters.title: Truce Clock
chapters.summary: POV: Commander Dae-Ho Rhee, Concordat liaison. Rhee arrives at the beacon under orders to decommission it before the fleet truce expires in nineteen days, taking custody of the Halcyon children as 'medical assets.' His private doubt about his orders humanizes him. The beat is bureaucratic menace — polite, lawful, and utterly determined to make the past stay buried.

chapters.title: What the Children Know
chapters.summary: POV: August. Under Rhee's supervision, August secretly tests the regressed crew, discovering their memories degrade toward childhood with each sleep cycle — the beacon's signal is the only thing holding their adult minds together. The girl who knew his name, Petra, gives him coordinates. The beat is desperate intimacy: becoming the children's protector while deceiving their jailer.

chapters.title: The Auditor's Confession, Interrupted
chapters.summary: POV: Ilsa Vey. Ilsa and August trace the auditor, Oren Castile, to a retirement habitat; he begins confessing to falsifying Meridian's records when his quarters are vented remotely, killing him mid-sentence. The beat is horror and guilt — August got close enough to the truth to get a man killed, and now knows the Concordat can reach anywhere.

chapters.title: Nineteen Becomes Fourteen
chapters.summary: POV: Rhee. Rhee's superiors move the deadline up, ordering the children transferred to a 'care facility' everyone understands is a disposal. Rhee stalls, filing objections he knows will be ignored. The beat is a loyal man's crisis of loyalty, as he realizes obedience and conscience have finally diverged beyond recall.

chapters.title: Signal Source
chapters.summary: POV: August. Following Petra's coordinates, August finds the beacon's true transmitter: not his antenna but a derelict relay at Meridian's actual location, still broadcasting the massacre's final minutes on loop. He witnesses the recording's first fragment — gunfire, a captain refusing an order. The beat is awe and grief, standing inside a crime scene preserved in light.

chapters.title: Eleven Thousand Names
chapters.summary: POV: Ilsa. At the relay, Ilsa recovers the victim manifest and recognizes her own adult signature among the dead — she was supposed to die at Meridian and doesn't know why she didn't. Survivor's guilt floods her child's body. The beat is mourning transformed into resolve: she will testify, whatever it costs her remaining self.

chapters.title: The Engineer's Price
chapters.summary: POV: August. The surviving suspect, engineer Maren Kole, agrees to authenticate the relay recording in exchange for passage off the fleet — and reveals the original August built the beacon deliberately, knowing he'd be murdered for it. The beat is devastating inheritance: August wasn't given a life, he was given a dead man's unfinished testimony.

chapters.title: Raid on the Relay
chapters.summary: POV: Rhee. Concordat forces, tipped off by a traitor among the children's caretakers, assault the relay to destroy it. Rhee, ordered to lead them, instead misdirects the strike team and buys August minutes. The beat is open rebellion — quiet, costly, irreversible — as Rhee burns his career to save evidence he half-doubts.

chapters.title: Betrayal in Small Voices
chapters.summary: POV: Ilsa. The traitor is revealed: young-bodied crewman Dev, whose regression erased his loyalty faster than his fear, trading the relay's location for a promised cure. Ilsa confronts him and cannot hate him. The beat is heartbreak over judgment — the enemy isn't wicked, just broken, which makes the Concordat's machinery more frightening, not less.

chapters.title: Half a Recording
chapters.summary: POV: August. The raid damaged the relay; only half the massacre recording survives, enough to prove violence but not who ordered it. Kole argues for fleeing with what they have; August refuses to abandon the victims' names. The beat is the loyalty-versus-truth theme made explicit: a partial truth might save them all, but a whole truth is what they owe the dead.

chapters.title: The Cure That Isn't
chapters.summary: POV: Ilsa. The 'care facility' is exposed as a memory-wipe clinic where regressed witnesses are made blank and adoptable. Ilsa infiltrates its records using skills her eight-year-old hands barely remember, confirming Dev's cure never existed. The beat is cold fury crystallizing into strategy — they must broadcast before the truce expires, or every witness becomes nobody.

chapters.title: Rhee's Defection
chapters.summary: POV: Rhee. Stripped of command for his stalling, Rhee delivers the final piece: the order that triggered the massacre came from the Concordat's founding council, meaning the government was born in cover-up. He defects openly, bringing authentication codes. The beat is a man choosing truth over thirty years of service, terrified and certain at once.

chapters.title: Assembly of the Accused
chapters.summary: POV: August. With four days left, August convenes an illegal quorum of fleet captains in the beacon's shadow, presenting the recording, the manifest, and Rhee's codes. The council's faction fights back with forged counter-evidence. The beat is rising tension at maximum — the room itself becomes the battlefield, and August's voice, cloned and therefore 'inadmissible,' seems doomed to fail.

chapters.title: The Original's Voice
chapters.summary: POV: Ilsa. The counter-evidence hinges on discrediting August as a copy; Ilsa plays the recovered first half of the recording, which contains the original August's dying testimony naming the council — making the clone the sole legitimate heir to admissible witness status. The beat is triumphant reversal: the thing used to erase August becomes the thing that authorizes him.

chapters.title: Expiration
chapters.summary: POV: August. The truce expires mid-session; Concordat warships converge on the beacon to silence everything at once. August makes the choice the original never could: he sacrifices the beacon's core to boost the massacre recording across every fleet channel simultaneously, unencrypted, undeniable. The beat is climax — annihilation of the past's prison at the cost of his home, his purpose, and nearly his life.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Light
chapters.summary: POV: Rhee. The broadcast fractures the Concordat; council members are arrested by their own fleets, and Rhee testifies at the tribunal he once would have enforced against August. The beat is exhausted vindication shadowed by loss — justice arrived, but Rhee knows how many blanks were already wiped and can never be filled.

chapters.title: Aging Forward
chapters.summary: POV: Ilsa. Freed from the Concordat's suppression field, the regressed crew begin aging forward again, memories stabilizing — though some losses are permanent, including most of what Dev betrayed them for. Ilsa, now seventeen and choosing to stay that way a while, forgives him imperfectly. The beat is bittersweet healing: time returns, but it returns changed.

chapters.title: Chosen Frequency
chapters.summary: POV: August. Rebuilding the beacon voluntarily — this time commissioned by the new provisional fleet — August stops investigating who he was and starts deciding who he is, keeping the original's case file open as memorial rather than inheritance. Petra asks to stay; he says yes. The beat is resolution and belonging: the signal continues, but now it carries names, and August answers to his own.
